## Learning Objectives {.objectives}

-   Distinguish between marketing, sales, and support.
-   Explain how a pitch differs from a list of features.
-   Describe places people will look for your software.

## What Marketing Is(n't)

-   Marketing means making sure the people you could help know you exist.
-   If you don't do this, someone else will (usually incorrectly).
-   Marketing is awareness: someone learns you exist.
-   Sales is adoption: someone goes from interested to using it.
-   Support is success: someone who uses it keeps being able to use it.

## Writing a Pitch

-   A pitch describes who has a problem, how they cope, and why you help.
-   It is not a list of features.
-   Test: can you explain the software in one sentence to someone outside your field?

## Pitches for Different Audiences

-   Different audiences need different descriptions.
    -   A grad student wants to know it runs and has examples.
    -   A senior researcher wants to know if it is maintained and citable.
    -   A program officer wants to know about impact and sustainability.
-   Things that cost almost nothing help the most.
    -   Add a `CITATION.cff` file, one working example, and one real use case.
    -   A working example converts curious visitors into users.

## Where to Go and What to Count

-   Preprint servers and software papers reach the right audience by default.
-   Mailing lists and chat communities are less formal.
-   The pitch form changes by channel.
-   The signal that matters most is being mentioned or cited in papers.
    -   Downloads and stars measure curiosity, not use.

## What about AI?

<ul>
  <li class="yes">LLMs can convert dense documentation into readable READMEs and blog posts</li>
  <li class="no">LLM-generated text often omits failure modes, limitations, and caveats</li>
  <li class="no">LLM pitches sound generic and lose the specific voice that persuades</li>
</ul>
